summary:
Kwara State stands under Nigeria's national framework, with no regional exception recorded. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), signed in January 2014, applies nationwide and makes same-sex sexual activity punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment under federal law; the sources describe the Criminal Code as operating in southern states and the Penal Code in northern states.

Kwara is not among the twelve states recorded as having adopted Sharia law — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — so no Sharia penal exposure is documented for the Ilorin area, and the federal statute supplies the operative framework.

The Act's reach extends well beyond sexual conduct. It voids same-sex unions and criminalises forming, operating or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations. Human Rights Watch, in 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe' (October 2016), records 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for participating in or supporting such organisations, a ban on same-sex cohabitation, and a ban on public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship.

A 2022 court ruling held Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the SSMPA unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide. The sources do not state which provisions remain operative or whether the ruling was appealed.

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is explicit and current. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated Nigeria travel advice, reported by SaharaReporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, states that same-sex activity carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, notes that some northern states under Sharia law can prescribe the death penalty, and confirms that the SSMPA reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

Trans visitors face lethal violence. The Nigerian transgender TikToker known as 'Abuja Area Mama', aged 33, was murdered in August 2024: her beaten body was found on a highway in Abuja and police opened an investigation. She had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life. The killing occurred in Abuja rather than Kwara, and it illustrates the national pattern rather than a Kwara-specific case.

Enforcement under the SSMPA takes the form of mass arrests and detention, recorded as common especially in northern states, alongside mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions across the country following the Act's passage. Human Rights Watch documents 21 young men arrested but never charged at an Ibadan birthday gathering. The report covers Nigeria nationally and names no Kwara-specific case; it documents the federal criminalisation and arbitrary enforcement that apply in Kwara.
tangentialFactors:
A decade-outcome assessment of the statute exists. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024), marking ten years of the SSMPA, finds that the law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.

Gender expression itself has been targeted legislatively. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing; the sources do not state whether any such proposal was enacted.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police use the law against people for how they appear. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility. The incident occurred in Lagos and functions as a single illustration of a national enforcement style.

Imprisonment of a prominent transgender woman raised placement questions. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
localsOnly:
Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk for residents as well as visitors. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.

Discrimination extends into employment. LGBTQ+ Nigerians interviewed a decade after the Act's passage report lost job prospects and a rise in attacks, and the passage of the 2014 law was followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions of LGBT people across the country.

Visibility in public carries a documented risk of police contact for appearance alone, as the Lagos 'looking gay' stop and extortion shows, and LGBTQ-friendly venues have faced closure: the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned.

Placement of transgender detainees is discretionary. Press coverage at Bobrisky's 2024 sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', and the October 2024 panel found that her maximum-security placement breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.
outOfScopeNotes:
Which of the two codes described in the sources — the Criminal Code operating in southern states or the Penal Code operating in northern states — supplies the operative text for offences in Kwara State is not stated in the sources consulted.

What the SSMPA provisions mean in practice after the 2022 ruling striking Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) as unconstitutional is unresolved here: the sources do not identify which sections remain enforceable, whether the judgment was appealed, or how prosecutors have adapted.

No Kwara-specific arrest, prosecution, venue closure or violent incident against a trans or gender-nonconforming person is documented in the sources. The Abuja Area Mama killing, the Ibadan and Lagos incidents, and the recorded mass arrests all occurred elsewhere in Nigeria.

The outcome of the police investigation into the August 2024 killing of 'Abuja Area Mama' is unresolved in the sources consulted.

Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing were enacted is not sourced. Availability of gender-affirming care, legal gender recognition, and document or marker change rules for visitors in Kwara are not sourced here.
